     9→
    10→**📖 Documentation**: [Click here](docs/README.md)
    11→
    12→**sqlgen** is a modern, type-safe ORM and SQL query generator for C++20, inspired by Python's [SQLAlchemy](https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy)/[SQLModel](https://github.com/fastapi/sqlmodel) and Rust's [Diesel](https://github.com/diesel-rs/diesel). It provides a fluent, composable interface for database operations with compile-time type checking and SQL injection protection.
    13→
    14→sqlgen is based on and tightly integrated with [reflect-cpp](https://github.com/getml/reflect-cpp), a C++-20 library for fast serialization, deserialization and validation using reflection, similar to pydantic in Python, serde in Rust, encoding in Go or aeson in Haskell.
    15→
    16→Together, reflect-cpp and sqlgen enable reliable and efficient ETL pipelines.
    17→
    18→## Features
    19→
    20→- 🔒 **Type Safety**: Compile-time validation of table schemas and queries
    21→- 🛡️ **SQL Injection Protection**: Built-in input validation and parameterized queries
    22→- 🔄 **Composable Queries**: Fluent interface for building complex queries
    23→- 🚀 **High Performance**: Efficient batch operations and prepared statements
    24→- 📦 **Modern C++**: Leverages C++20 features for a clean, expressive API
    25→- 🔌 **Multiple Backends**: Support for PostgreSQL and SQLite
    26→- 🔍 **Reflection Integration**: Seamless integration with [reflect-cpp](https://github.com/getml/reflect-cpp) 
    27→
    28→## Supported databases 
    29→
    30→The following table lists the databases currently supported by sqlgen and the underlying libraries used:
    31→
    32→| Database      | Library                                                                  | Version      | License       | Remarks                                              |
    33→|---------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------|---------------| -----------------------------------------------------|
    34→| MySQL/MariaDB | [libmariadb](https://github.com/mariadb-corporation/mariadb-connector-c) | >= 3.4.5     | LGPL          |                                                      |
    35→| PostgreSQL    | [libpq](https://github.com/postgres/postgres)                            | >= 16.4      | PostgreSQL    | Will work for all libpq-compatible databases         |
    36→| sqlite        | [sqlite](https://sqlite.org/index.html)                                  | >= 3.49.1    | Public Domain |                                                      |

    38→## Quick Start
    39→
    40→### Installation using vcpkg
    41→
    42→1. Make sure you have the required dependencies installed (skip this step on Windows):
    43→```bash
    44→sudo apt-get install autoconf bison flex # Linux (Ubuntu, Debian, ...)
    45→brew install autoconf bison flex # macOS
    46→```
    47→
    48→2. Set up vcpkg:
    49→```bash
    50→git submodule update --init
    51→./vcpkg/bootstrap-vcpkg.sh  # Linux, macOS
    52→./vcpkg/bootstrap-vcpkg.bat # Windows
    53→```
    54→
    55→3. Build the library:
    56→```bash
    57→cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_CXX_STANDARD=20 -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
    58→cmake --build build -j 4  # gcc, clang
    59→cmake --build build --config Release -j 4  # MSVC
    60→```
    61→
    62→This will build the static library. To build the shared library 
    63→add `-DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON -DVCPKG_TARGET_TRIPLET=...` to the first line.
    64→Run `./vcpkg/vcpkg help triplets` to view all supported triplets. 
    65→Common triplets for shared libraries are `x64-linux-dynamic`, 
    66→`arm64-osx-dynamic` or `x64-osx-dynamic`.   
    67→
    68→Add `-DSQLGEN_MYSQL=ON` to support MySQL/MariaDB.
    69→
    70→4. Include in your CMake project:
    71→```cmake
    72→find_package(sqlgen REQUIRED)
    73→target_link_libraries(your_target PRIVATE sqlgen::sqlgen)
    74→```
    75→
    76→### Installation using Conan
    77→
    78→1. Install Conan (assuming you have Python and pipx installed):
    79→
    80→```bash
    81→pipx install conan
    82→conan profile detect
    83→```
    84→
    85→For older versions of pip, you can also use `pip` instead of `pipx`.
    86→
    87→2. Build the library:
    88→
    89→```bash
    90→conan build . --build=missing -s compiler.cppstd=gnu20
    91→```
    92→
    93→This will build the static library. To build the shared library,
    94→add `-o */*:shared=True`. 
    95→
    96→Add `-o sqlgen/*:with_mysql=True` to support MySQL/MariaDB.
    97→
    98→3. Include in your CMake project:
    99→```cmake
   100→find_package(sqlgen REQUIRED)
   101→target_link_libraries(your_target PRIVATE sqlgen::sqlgen)
   102→```
   103→
   104→You can call `conan inspect .` to get an overview of the supported options.

   106→## Usage Examples
   107→
   108→### Hello World
   109→
   110→```cpp
   111→#include <sqlgen/sqlite.hpp>
   112→#include <iostream>
   113→
   114→struct User {
   115→    std::string name;
   116→    int age;
   117→};
   118→
   119→int main() {
   120→    // Connect to SQLite database
   121→    const auto conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("test.db");
   122→    
   123→    // Create and insert a user
   124→    const auto user = User{.name = "John", .age = 30};
   125→    sqlgen::write(conn, user);
   126→    
   127→    // Read all users
   128→    const auto users = sqlgen::read<std::vector<User>>(conn).value();
   129→    
   130→    for (const auto& u : users) {
   131→        std::cout << u.name << " is " << u.age << " years old\n";
   132→    }
   133→}
   134→```
   135→
   136→### Connecting to a Database
   137→
   138→```cpp
   139→#include <sqlgen/postgres.hpp>
   140→
   141→// PostgreSQL connection
   142→const auto credentials = sqlgen::postgres::Credentials{
   143→    .user = "username",
   144→    .password = "password",
   145→    .host = "localhost",
   146→    .dbname = "mydb",
   147→    .port = 5432
   148→};
   149→
   150→const auto conn = sqlgen::postgres::connect(credentials);
   151→
   152→// SQLite connection
   153→const auto sqlite_conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("database.db");
   154→```
   155→
   156→### Defining Models
   157→
   158→```cpp
   159→struct Person {
   160→    std::string first_name;
   161→    std::string last_name;
   162→    uint32_t age;
   163→    std::optional<std::string> email;  // Nullable field
   164→};
   165→```
   166→
   167→### Inserting Data
   168→
   169→```cpp
   170→const auto people = std::vector<Person>({
   171→    Person{.first_name = "Homer", .last_name = "Simpson", .age = 45},
   172→    Person{.first_name = "Marge", .last_name = "Simpson", .age = 42}
   173→});
   174→
   175→// Automatically creates table if it doesn't exist
   176→// (recall that the table is fully defined at compile time)
   177→const auto result = sqlgen::write(conn, people);
   178→
   179→if (!result) {
   180→    std::cerr << "Error: " << result.error().what() << std::endl;
   181→}
   182→```
   183→
   184→Or:
   185→
   186→```cpp
   187→...
   188→
   189→// write(...) abstracts these steps away, but
   190→// if you prefer more granular control, you
   191→// can use sqlgen::insert.
   192→const auto result = begin_transaction(conn)
   193→                        .and_then(create_table<Person> | if_not_exists)
   194→                        .and_then(insert(std::ref(people)))
   195→                        .and_then(commit);
   196→
   197→...
   198→```
   199→
   200→Generated SQL:
   201→```sql
   202→BEGIN TRANSACTION;
   203→CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "Person" (
   204→    "first_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
   205→    "last_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
   206→    "age" INTEGER NOT NULL,
   207→    "email" TEXT
   208→);
   209→
   210→INSERT INTO "Person" ("first_name", "last_name", "age", "email") 
   211→VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?);
   212→COMMIT;
   213→```
   214→
   215→### Querying Data
   216→
   217→```cpp
   218→#include <rfl/json.hpp>
   219→#include <sqlgen/postgres.hpp>
   220→
   221→using namespace sqlgen;
   222→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
   223→
   224→// Build a query for adults, ordered by age
   225→const auto query = read<std::vector<Person>> |
   226→                   where("age"_c >= 18) |
   227→                   order_by("age"_c.desc(), "last_name"_c) |
   228→                   limit(10);
   229→
   230→// Execute the query
   231→const auto result = query(conn);
   232→
   233→if (result) {
   234→    // Print results as JSON
   235→    std::cout << rfl::json::write(*result) << std::endl;
   236→} else {
   237→    std::cerr << "Error: " << result.error().what() << std::endl;
   238→}
   239→```
   240→
   241→Generated SQL:
   242→```sql
   243→SELECT "first_name", "last_name", "age", "email"
   244→FROM "Person"
   245→WHERE "age" >= 18
   246→ORDER BY "age" DESC, "last_name"
   247→LIMIT 10;
   248→```
   249→
   250→### Grouping and Aggregating Data
   251→
   252→```cpp
   253→using namespace sqlgen;
   254→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
   255→
   256→struct Children {
   257→    std::string last_name;
   258→    int num_children;
   259→    int max_age;
   260→    int min_age;
   261→    int sum_age;
   262→};
   263→
   264→const auto get_children = select_from<Person>(
   265→    "last_name"_c,
   266→    count().as<"num_children">(),
   267→    max("age"_c).as<"max_age">(),
   268→    min("age"_c).as<"min_age">(),
   269→    sum("age"_c).as<"sum_age">(),
   270→) | where("age"_c < 18) | group_by("last_name"_c) | to<std::vector<Children>>;
   271→
   272→const std::vector<Children> children = get_children(conn).value();
   273→```
   274→
   275→Generated SQL:
   276→```sql
   277→SELECT 
   278→    "last_name",
   279→    COUNT(*) as "num_children",
   280→    MAX("age") as "max_age",
   281→    MIN("age") as "min_age",
   282→    SUM("age") as "sum_age"
   283→FROM "Person"
   284→WHERE "age" < 18
   285→GROUP BY "last_name";
   286→```

   288→### Joining data
   289→
   290→```cpp
   291→using namespace sqlgen;
   292→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
   293→
   294→struct ParentAndChild {
   295→    std::string last_name;
   296→    std::string first_name_parent;
   297→    std::string first_name_child;
   298→    double parent_age_at_birth;
   299→};
   300→
   301→const auto get_people =
   302→  select_from<Person, "t1">(
   303→      "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
   304→      "first_name"_t1 | as<"first_name_parent">,
   305→      "first_name"_t3 | as<"first_name_child">,
   306→      ("age"_t1 - "age"_t3) | as<"parent_age_at_birth">) |
   307→  inner_join<Relationship, "t2">("id"_t1 == "parent_id"_t2) |
   308→  inner_join<Person, "t3">("id"_t3 == "child_id"_t2) |
   309→  order_by("id"_t1, "id"_t3) | to<std::vector<ParentAndChild>>;
   310→```
   311→
   312→Generated SQL:
   313→```sql
   314→SELECT t1."last_name" AS "last_name", 
   315→       t1."first_name" AS "first_name_parent", 
   316→       t3."first_name" AS "first_name_child", 
   317→       t1."age" - t3."age" AS "parent_age_at_birth" 
   318→FROM "Person" t1 
   319→INNER JOIN "Relationship" t2 
   320→ON t1."id" = t2."parent_id" 
   321→INNER JOIN "Person" t3
   322→ON t3."id" = t2."child_id" 
   323→ORDER BY t1."id", t3."id"
   324→```

   326→### Nested joins
   327→
   328→```cpp

   330→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
   331→
   332→struct ParentAndChild {
   333→    std::string last_name;
   334→    std::string first_name_parent;
   335→    std::string first_name_child;
   336→    double parent_age_at_birth;
   337→};
   338→
   339→// First, create a subquery
   340→const auto get_children =
   341→  select_from<Relationship, "t1">("parent_id"_t1 | as<"id">,
   342→                                  "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name">,
   343→                                  "age"_t2 | as<"age">) |
   344→  inner_join<Person, "t2">("id"_t2 == "child_id"_t1);
   345→
   346→// Then use it as a source for another query
   347→const auto get_people =
   348→  select_from<Person, "t1">(
   349→      "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
   350→      "first_name"_t1 | as<"first_name_parent">,
   351→      "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name_child">,
   352→      ("age"_t1 - "age"_t2) | as<"parent_age_at_birth">) |
   353→  inner_join<"t2">(
   354→    get_children, // Use the subquery as the source
   355→    "id"_t1 == "id"_t2) | 
   356→  order_by("id"_t1, "id"_t2) | to<std::vector<ParentAndChild>>;
   357→```

   362→    t1."first_name" AS "first_name_parent", 
   363→    t2."first_name" AS "first_name_child", 
   364→    t1."age" - t2."age" AS "parent_age_at_birth"

   367→    SELECT t1."parent_id" AS "id", 
   368→           t2."first_name" AS "first_name", 
   369→           t2."age" AS "age"

   429→### Type Safety and SQL Injection Protection
   430→
   431→sqlgen provides comprehensive compile-time checks and runtime protection:
   432→
   433→```cpp
   434→// Compile-time error: No such column "color"
   435→const auto query = read<std::vector<Person>> |
   436→                   where("color"_c == "blue");
   437→
   438→// Compile-time error: Cannot compare column "age" to a string 
   439→const auto query = read<std::vector<Person>> |
   440→                   where("age"_c == "Homer");
   441→
   442→// Compile-time error: "age" must be aggregated or included in GROUP BY 
   443→const auto query = select_from<Person>(
   444→    "last_name"_c,
   445→    "age"_c 
   446→) | group_by("last_name"_c);
   447→
   448→// Compile-time error: Cannot add string and int 
   449→const auto query = select_from<Person>(
   450→    "last_name"_c + "age"_c 
   451→);
   452→
   453→// Runtime protection against SQL injection
   454→std::vector<Person> get_people(const auto& conn, 
   455→                              const sqlgen::AlphaNumeric& first_name) {
   456→    using namespace sqlgen;
   457→    return (read<std::vector<Person>> | 
   458→            where("first_name"_c == first_name))(conn).value();
   459→}
   460→
   461→// This will be rejected
   462→get_people(conn, "Homer' OR '1'='1");  // SQL injection attempt

1→# Defining tables
     2→
     3→`sqlgen` provides a type-safe way to define database tables using C++ structs. It automatically handles table creation, schema management, and nullability through C++ types.
     4→
     5→## Usage
     6→
     7→### Basic Table Definition
     8→
     9→Define a table using a simple C++ struct:
    10→
    11→```cpp
    12→struct People {
    13→    std::string first_name;
    14→    std::string last_name;
    15→    uint age;
    16→};
    17→```
    18→
    19→When you write data to this table, it will be automatically created if it doesn't exist:
    20→
    21→```cpp
    22→const auto people = std::vector<People>(...);
    23→const auto result = sqlgen::write(conn, people);
    24→```
    25→
    26→This generates SQL similar to:
    27→
    28→```sql
    29→CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "People"(
    30→    "first_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
    31→    "last_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
    32→    "age" INTEGER NOT NULL
    33→);
    34→```
    35→
    36→### Custom Table Names
    37→
    38→Override the default table name using a static member:
    39→
    40→```cpp
    41→struct People {
    42→    constexpr static const char* tablename = "PEOPLE";
    43→    
    44→    std::string first_name;
    45→    std::string last_name;
    46→    uint age;
    47→};
    48→```
    49→
    50→This generates SQL with the custom table name:
    51→
    52→```sql
    53→CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "PEOPLE"(
    54→    "first_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
    55→    "last_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
    56→    "age" INTEGER NOT NULL
    57→);
    58→```
    59→
    60→### Custom Schemas
    61→
    62→Define a table within a specific schema:
    63→
    64→```cpp
    65→struct People {
    66→    constexpr static const char* schema = "my_schema";
    67→    
    68→    std::string first_name;
    69→    std::string last_name;
    70→    uint age;
    71→};
    72→```
    73→
    74→This generates SQL with the schema specification:
    75→
    76→```sql
    77→CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "my_schema"."People"(
    78→    "first_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
    79→    "last_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
    80→    "age" INTEGER NOT NULL
    81→);
    82→```
    83→
    84→### Nullable Fields
    85→
    86→As we have seen, all columns are non-nullable by default. But what if we do want
    87→nullability?
    88→
    89→As with reflect-cpp, `std::optional`, `std::shared_ptr` and `std::unique_ptr` are interpreted as nullable types,
    90→but it is strongly recommended that you use `std::optional`.
    91→
    92→So you can create nullable fields as follows:
    93→
    94→```cpp
    95→struct People {
    96→    rfl::PrimaryKey<std::string> first_name;
    97→    std::string last_name;
    98→    std::optional<uint> age;
    99→};
   100→```
   101→
   102→## Notes
   103→
   104→- All fields are non-nullable by default
   105→- Nullable fields can be defined using:
   106→  - `std::optional<T>` (strongly recommended)
   107→  - `std::shared_ptr<T>`
   108→  - `std::unique_ptr<T>`
   109→- Use `std::nullopt` or `nullptr` to represent NULL values
   110→- The exact SQL generated may vary between database dialects
   111→- Table names are inferred from struct names by default
   112→- Custom table names and schemas can be specified using static members
   113→

1→# `sqlgen::PrimaryKey`
     2→
     3→`sqlgen::PrimaryKey` is used to indicate which key should be a primary key.
     4→
     5→## Usage
     6→
     7→### Basic Definition
     8→
     9→Define a primary key field in your struct:
    10→
    11→```cpp
    12→struct People {
    13→    sqlgen::PrimaryKey<std::string> first_name;
    14→    std::string last_name;
    15→    uint age;
    16→};
    17→```
    18→
    19→This generates the following SQL schema:
    20→
    21→```sql
    22→CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "People"(
    23→    "first_name" TEXT NOT NULL, 
    24→    "last_name"  TEXT NOT NULL, 
    25→    "age"        INTEGER NOT NULL,
    26→    PRIMARY_KEY("first_name")
    27→);
    28→```
    29→
    30→### Auto-incrementing Primary Keys
    31→
    32→You can define an auto-incrementing primary key by providing `sqlgen::auto_incr` as the second template argument to `sqlgen::PrimaryKey`. The underlying type of an auto-incrementing primary key must be an integral type.
    33→
    34→```cpp
    35→struct Person {
    36→  sqlgen::PrimaryKey<uint32_t, sqlgen::auto_incr> id;
    37→  std::string first_name;
    38→  std::string last_name;
    39→  int age;
    40→};
    41→```
    42→
    43→This will produce SQL schema with an auto-incrementing primary key. For instance, for PostgreSQL it will generate:
    44→
    45→```sql
    46→CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "Person"(
    47→    "id"         INTEGER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY,
    48→    "first_name" TEXT NOT NULL, 
    49→    "last_name"  TEXT NOT NULL, 
    50→    "age"        INTEGER NOT NULL,
    51→    PRIMARY KEY("id")
    52→);
    53→```
    54→
    55→And for SQLite:
    56→
    57→```sql
    58→CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "Person"(
    59→    "id"         INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, 
    60→    "first_name" TEXT NOT NULL, 
    61→    "last_name"  TEXT NOT NULL, 
    62→    "age"        INTEGER NOT NULL
    63→);
    64→```
    65→
    66→When you insert an object with an auto-incrementing primary key, you do not need to provide a value for the key field. The database will automatically assign a unique, incrementing value.
    67→
    68→```cpp
    69→auto homer = Person{.first_name = "Homer", .last_name = "Simpson", .age = 45};
    70→// The 'id' field is not set.
    71→
    72→// After writing to the database and reading it back, the 'id' will be populated.
    73→auto people = std::vector<Person>({homer});
    74→auto result = conn.and_then(sqlgen::write(std::ref(people)))
    75→                  .and_then(sqlgen::read<std::vector<Person>>())
    76→                  .value();
    77→
    78→// result[0].id will now have a value, for instance 1.
    79→```
    80→
    81→### Assignment and Access
    82→
    83→Assign values to primary key fields:
    84→
    85→```cpp
    86→const auto person = People{
    87→    .first_name = "Homer",
    88→    .last_name = "Simpson",
    89→    .age = 45
    90→};
    91→```
    92→
    93→Access the underlying value using any of these methods:
    94→
    95→```cpp
    96→person.first_name();
    97→person.first_name.get();
    98→person.first_name.value();
    99→```
   100→
   101→## Notes
   102→
   103→- The template parameter specifies the type of the primary key field
   104→- Primary key fields are automatically marked as NOT NULL in the generated SQL
   105→- Auto-incrementing primary keys must have an integral type.
   106→- The class supports:
   107→  - Direct value assignment
   108→  - Multiple access methods for the underlying value
   109→  - Reflection for SQL operations
   110→  - Move and copy semantics
   111→- Primary keys can be used with any supported SQL data type
   112→
   113→

1→# `sqlgen::Timestamp`
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen::Timestamp` class provides a type-safe way to handle SQL timestamp fields in C++. It supports both regular timestamps and timestamps with time zones, with format validation at runtime. The class is essentially a wrapper around `std::tm` that adds format validation and SQL integration.
     4→
     5→## Usage
     6→
     7→### Basic Definition
     8→
     9→Define a timestamp field in your struct with a specific format:
    10→
    11→```cpp
    12→struct Person {
    13→    sqlgen::PrimaryKey<uint32_t> id;
    14→    std::string first_name;
    15→    std::string last_name;
    16→    sqlgen::Timestamp<"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"> birthdate;  // Regular timestamp
    17→    sqlgen::Timestamp<"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S%z"> created_at;  // Timestamp with timezone
    18→};
    19→```
    20→
    21→This generates the following SQL schema:
    22→
    23→```sql
    24→CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "Person"(
    25→    "id" INTEGER NOT NULL,
    26→    "first_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
    27→    "last_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
    28→    "birthdate" TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    29→    "created_at" TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE NOT NULL,
    30→    PRIMARY KEY ("id")
    31→);
    32→```
    33→
    34→### Construction and Assignment
    35→
    36→Create and assign timestamp values:
    37→
    38→```cpp
    39→// Direct string assignment
    40→Person person{
    41→    .id = 1,
    42→    .first_name = "Homer",
    43→    .last_name = "Simpson",
    44→    .birthdate = "1989-12-17 12:00:00",
    45→    .created_at = "2024-03-20 15:30:00+0000"
    46→};
    47→
    48→// Create from std::tm
    49→std::tm birth_tm = std::tm{};
    50→birth_tm.tm_year = 89;  // Years since 1900
    51→birth_tm.tm_mon = 11;   // 0-11 for months
    52→birth_tm.tm_mday = 17;  // Day of month
    53→birth_tm.tm_hour = 12;
    54→birth_tm.tm_min = 0;
    55→birth_tm.tm_sec = 0;
    56→sqlgen::Timestamp<"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"> birthdate(birth_tm);
    57→
    58→// Safe construction with error handling
    59→auto result = sqlgen::Timestamp<"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S">::from_string("1989-12-17 12:00:00");
    60→if (result) {
    61→    auto birthdate = result.value();
    62→    // Use birthdate...
    63→} else {
    64→    // Handle error...
    65→}
    66→```
    67→
    68→### Accessing Values
    69→
    70→Access the timestamp value in different formats:
    71→
    72→```cpp
    73→const auto person = Person{
    74→    .birthdate = "1989-12-17 12:00:00"
    75→};
    76→
    77→// Get as formatted string
    78→const std::string& str_value2 = person.birthdate.str(); // Returns "1989-12-17 12:00:00"
    79→
    80→// Get as std::tm for time operations
    81→const std::tm& tm_value = person.birthdate.tm();  // Direct access to underlying std::tm
    82→```
    83→
    84→### Time Zone Support
    85→
    86→The class supports both regular timestamps and timestamps with time zones:
    87→
    88→```cpp
    89→// Regular timestamp (without timezone)
    90→sqlgen::Timestamp<"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"> local_time;
    91→
    92→// Timestamp with timezone
    93→sqlgen::Timestamp<"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S%z"> utc_time;
    94→
    95→// Examples
    96→local_time = "2024-03-20 15:30:00";  // Local time
    97→utc_time = "2024-03-20 15:30:00+0000";  // UTC time with offset
    98→```
    99→
   100→## Format Specification
   101→
   102→The timestamp format is specified using a template parameter that follows the strftime format specifiers. This format is significant because:
   103→
   104→1. It defines the expected string format when reading timestamps from the database
   105→2. It determines how timestamps are formatted when writing to the database
   106→3. It enforces consistency between your C++ code and database storage
   107→
   108→For example, with this definition:
   109→```cpp
   110→struct Person {
   111→    sqlgen::Timestamp<"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"> birthdate;
   112→};
   113→```
   114→
   115→- When reading from the database, the timestamp must be in the format "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS"
   116→- When writing to the database, the timestamp will be formatted as "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS"
   117→- Any attempt to assign a string in a different format will throw a runtime error
   118→
   119→The most importand supported format specifiers are:
   120→
   121→- `%Y`: Year with century (e.g., 2024)
   122→- `%m`: Month (01-12)
   123→- `%d`: Day of month (01-31)
   124→- `%H`: Hour in 24h format (00-23)
   125→- `%M`: Minute (00-59)
   126→- `%S`: Second (00-59)
   127→- `%z`: Timezone offset (e.g., +0000, -0500)
   128→
   129→Please refer to https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/chrono/c/strftime for a comprehensive list of supported format specifiers.
   130→
   131→Common format patterns:
   132→- `"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"` for regular timestamps
   133→- `"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S%z"` for timestamps with timezone
   134→
   135→### Database Integration
   136→
   137→The format parameter ensures type safety and consistency in database operations:
   138→
   139→```cpp
   140→// Reading from database
   141→const auto people = sqlgen::read<std::vector<Person>>(conn).value();
   142→// All timestamps in 'people' will be in the format "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"
   143→
   144→// Writing to database
   145→const auto person = Person{
   146→    .birthdate = "1989-12-17 12:00:00"  // Must match the format
   147→};
   148→sqlgen::write(conn, person);  // Will be stored in the database in this format
   149→
   150→// Querying with timestamps
   151→const auto query = sqlgen::read<std::vector<Person>> | 
   152→                  where("birthdate"_c == "1989-12-17 12:00:00");  // Must match the format
   153→```
   154→
   155→This format validation helps prevent:
   156→- Data corruption from inconsistent timestamp formats
   157→- SQL injection by validating the format before database operations
   158→- Runtime errors from malformed timestamp strings
   159→
   160→## Notes
   161→
   162→- The template parameter `_format` specifies the expected timestamp format
   163→- Format validation occurs at runtime when values are assigned
   164→- The class is a wrapper around `std::tm` that adds:
   165→  - Format validation
   166→  - String conversion
   167→  - SQL integration
   168→  - Type safety
   169→- The class supports:
   170→  - Direct string assignment with format validation
   171→  - Construction from `std::tm`
   172→  - Safe construction with error handling via `from_string`
   173→  - Multiple access methods for the underlying value
   174→  - Direct access to the underlying `std::tm` via `tm()`
   175→  - Reflection for SQL operations
   176→  - Move and copy semantics
   177→- Timezone support varies by database:
   178→  - PostgreSQL supports both regular timestamps and timestamps with timezone
   179→  - SQLite treats all timestamps as UTC
   180→- The class uses the underlying `rfl::Timestamp` implementation for core functionality
   181→- All string operations are validated against the specified format
   182→- Invalid format strings will throw a runtime error
   183→- The class provides both compile-time and runtime safety

     3→The `sqlgen::group_by` interface provides a type-safe way to group and aggregate data in SQL queries. It supports various aggregation functions like `count`, `avg`, `sum`, `min`, `max`, and `count_distinct`.
     4→
     5→## Usage
     6→
     7→### Basic Aggregations
     8→
     9→Perform aggregations without grouping:
    10→
    11→```cpp
    12→using namespace sqlgen;
    13→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    14→
    15→struct Children {
    16→    int num_children;
    17→    int num_last_names;
    18→    double avg_age;
    19→    double max_age;
    20→    double min_age;
    21→    double sum_age;
    22→};
    23→
    24→const auto get_children = select_from<Person>(
    25→    avg("age"_c).as<"avg_age">(),
    26→    count().as<"num_children">(),
    27→    max("age"_c).as<"max_age">(),
    28→    min("age"_c).as<"min_age">(),
    29→    sum("age"_c).as<"sum_age">(),
    30→    count_distinct("last_name"_c).as<"num_last_names">()
    31→) | where("age"_c < 18) | to<Children>;
    32→
    33→const auto children = sqlite::connect()
    34→    .and_then(get_children)
    35→    .value();
    36→```
    37→
    38→This generates the following SQL:
    39→
    40→```sql
    41→SELECT 
    42→    AVG("age") as "avg_age",
    43→    COUNT(*) as "num_children",
    44→    MAX("age") as "max_age",
    45→    MIN("age") as "min_age",
    46→    SUM("age") as "sum_age",
    47→    COUNT(DISTINCT "last_name") as "num_last_names"
    48→FROM "Person"
    49→WHERE "age" < 18;
    50→```
    51→
    52→### Group By with Aggregations
    53→
    54→Group data and perform aggregations:
    55→
    56→```cpp
    57→using namespace sqlgen;
    58→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    59→
    60→struct Children {
    61→    std::string last_name;
    62→    int num_children;
    63→    int num_last_names;
    64→    double avg_age;
    65→    double max_age;
    66→    double min_age;
    67→    double sum_age;
    68→};
    69→
    70→const auto get_children = select_from<Person>(
    71→    "last_name"_c,
    72→    avg("age"_c).as<"avg_age">(),
    73→    count().as<"num_children">(),
    74→    max("age"_c).as<"max_age">(),
    75→    min("age"_c).as<"min_age">(),
    76→    sum("age"_c).as<"sum_age">(),
    77→    count_distinct("last_name"_c).as<"num_last_names">()
    78→) | where("age"_c < 18) | group_by("last_name"_c) | to<std::vector<Children>>;
    79→
    80→const auto children = sqlite::connect()
    81→    .and_then(drop<Person> | if_exists)
    82→    .and_then(write(std::ref(people)))
    83→    .and_then(get_children)
    84→    .value();
    85→```
    86→
    87→This generates the following SQL:
    88→
    89→```sql
    90→SELECT 
    91→    "last_name",
    92→    AVG("age") as "avg_age",
    93→    COUNT(*) as "num_children",
    94→    MAX("age") as "max_age",
    95→    MIN("age") as "min_age",
    96→    SUM("age") as "sum_age",
    97→    COUNT(DISTINCT "last_name") as "num_last_names"
    98→FROM "Person"
    99→WHERE "age" < 18
   100→GROUP BY "last_name";
   101→```
   102→
   103→## Available Aggregation Functions
   104→
   105→The following aggregation functions are available:
   106→
   107→- `count()` - Counts all rows
   108→- `count_distinct(col)` - Counts distinct values in a column
   109→- `avg(col)` - Calculates average of a column
   110→- `sum(col)` - Calculates sum of a column
   111→- `max(col)` - Finds maximum value in a column
   112→- `min(col)` - Finds minimum value in a column
   113→
   114→Each aggregation function can be aliased using the `.as<"alias">()` syntax.
   115→
   116→## Aggregating Nullable Values
   117→
   118→When working with nullable columns (e.g., `std::optional<T>`), it's important to understand how aggregations handle null values:
   119→
   120→1. The result of aggregating a nullable column must also be nullable (e.g., `std::optional<double>`)
   121→2. Null values are excluded from aggregation calculations
   122→3. If all values in a group are null, the aggregation result will be null
   123→
   124→### Example with Nullable Values
   125→
   126→```cpp
   127→struct Person {
   128→    sqlgen::PrimaryKey<uint32_t> id;
   129→    std::string first_name;
   130→    std::string last_name;
   131→    std::optional<double> age;  // Nullable age field
   132→};
   133→
   134→struct Children {
   135→    int num_children;           // Non-nullable count
   136→    int num_last_names;        // Non-nullable count
   137→    std::optional<double> avg_age;  // Nullable aggregation
   138→    std::optional<double> max_age;  // Nullable aggregation
   139→    std::optional<double> min_age;  // Nullable aggregation
   140→    std::optional<double> sum_age;  // Nullable aggregation
   141→};
   142→
   143→const auto get_children = select_from<Person>(
   144→    avg("age"_c).as<"avg_age">(),      // Results in std::optional<double>
   145→    count().as<"num_children">(),      // Results in int (non-nullable)
   146→    max("age"_c).as<"max_age">(),      // Results in std::optional<double>
   147→    min("age"_c).as<"min_age">(),      // Results in std::optional<double>
   148→    sum("age"_c).as<"sum_age">(),      // Results in std::optional<double>
   149→    count_distinct("last_name"_c).as<"num_last_names">()
   150→) | where("age"_c < 18 or "age"_c.is_null()) | to<Children>;
   151→```
   152→
   153→In this example:
   154→- The `age` column is nullable (`std::optional<double>`)
   155→- All aggregations of `age` result in nullable values (`std::optional<double>`)
   156→- The `count()` and `count_distinct()` functions return non-nullable integers
   157→- The `where` clause includes both non-null values less than 18 and null values
   158→- If all values in a group are null, the aggregation results (avg, max, min, sum) will be null
   159→
   160→### Important Notes
   161→
   162→- Always use nullable types (`std::optional<T>`) for aggregated values when the source column is nullable
   163→- Count operations (`count()`, `count_distinct()`) always return non-nullable integers
   164→- Null values are excluded from aggregation calculations (avg, sum, max, min)
   165→- When all values in a group are null, the aggregation result will be null
   166→- The type system will enforce these rules at compile time
   167→
   168→## The `.as` Operator
   169→
   170→The `.as` operator allows you to alias columns and expressions in your SQL queries. This is particularly important when mapping query results to C++ structs, as the field names in your struct must match the aliases used in the query.
   171→
   172→### Usage
   173→
   174→You can use `.as` in several ways:
   175→
   176→```cpp
   177→// Method 1: Using the .as() member function
   178→"field1"_c.as<"field">()
   179→
   180→// Method 2: Using the pipe operator with as
   181→"nullable"_c | as<"nullable_field">
   182→
   183→// Method 3: Using as directly with values
   184→as<"one">(1)
   185→"hello" | as<"hello">
   186→```
   187→
   188→### Important Notes
   189→
   190→- Field names in your result struct must exactly match the aliases used in the query
   191→- Fields are matched by name, not by order
   192→- You can alias any column, expression, or literal value
   193→- The alias must be a string literal (using the `as<"alias">` syntax)
   194→
   195→### Example
   196→
   197→```cpp
   198→struct Result {
   199→    std::string field;           // Matches "field1"_c.as<"field">()
   200→    double avg_field2;           // Matches avg("field2"_c).as<"avg_field2">()
   201→    std::optional<std::string> nullable_field;  // Matches "nullable"_c | as<"nullable_field">
   202→    int one;                     // Matches as<"one">(1)
   203→    std::string hello;           // Matches "hello" | as<"hello">
   204→};
   205→
   206→const auto query = select_from<TestTable>(
   207→    "field1"_c.as<"field">(),
   208→    avg("field2"_c).as<"avg_field2">(),
   209→    "nullable"_c | as<"nullable_field">,
   210→    as<"one">(1),
   211→    "hello" | as<"hello">
   212→) | to<Result>;
   213→```
   214→
   215→In this example, each field in the `Result` struct must have a name that matches one of the aliases used in the query. The order of the fields in the struct doesn't matter, but the names must match exactly.
   216→
   217→## Notes
   218→
   219→- The `group_by` clause must be used before `order_by` or `limit` clauses
   220→- You cannot use `group_by` multiple times in the same query
   221→- Aggregation functions can be used with or without `group_by`
   222→- The result type must match the structure of your select statement. Note that fields are matched by name, not order.
   223→- All aggregations are type-safe and will map to appropriate SQL types
   224→- The `Result<...>` type provides error handling; use `.value()` to extract the result (will throw an exception if there's an error) or handle errors as needed
   225→

    10→namespace sqlgen {
    11→
    12→template <class T>
    13→class Range;
    14→
    15→/// This exists mainly for user-friendliness: We want people to be able
    16→/// to pass Range<T> to read without having to worry about connector-specific
    17→/// iterators.
    18→template <class T>
    19→struct Range {
    20→  using value_type = Result<T>;
    21→};
    22→
    23→/// This class is meant to provide a way to iterate through the data in the
    24→/// database efficiently that is compatible with std::ranges.
    25→template <class IteratorType>
    26→  requires std::input_iterator<IteratorType>
    27→class Range<IteratorType> {
    28→ public:
    29→  using value_type = typename IteratorType::value_type;
    30→
    31→  struct End {};
    32→
    33→  Range(const IteratorType& _it) : it_(_it) {}
    34→
    35→  ~Range() = default;
    36→
    37→  auto begin() const { return it_; }
    38→
    39→  auto end() const { return typename IteratorType::End{}; }
    40→
    41→ private:
    42→  /// The underlying database iterator.
    43→  IteratorType it_;
    44→};
    45→
    46→}  // namespace sqlgen
    47→
    48→#endif

1→# `sqlgen::select_from`
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen::select_from` function provides a type-safe, composable interface for building SQL SELECT queries in C++. It supports selecting from tables, subqueries, and complex nested queries with full support for joins, filtering, grouping, ordering, and result type conversion.
     4→
     5→## Basic Usage
     6→
     7→### Selecting from a Table
     8→
     9→```cpp
    10→using namespace sqlgen;
    11→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    12→
    13→struct Person {
    14→    sqlgen::PrimaryKey<uint32_t> id;
    15→    std::string first_name;
    16→    std::string last_name;
    17→    int age;
    18→};
    19→
    20→// Select specific columns
    21→const auto query = select_from<Person>("first_name"_c, "last_name"_c, "age"_c);
    22→
    23→// Execute the query
    24→const auto people = sqlite::connect()
    25→    .and_then(query | to<std::vector<Person>>)
    26→    .value();
    27→```
    28→
    29→This generates:
    30→```sql
    31→SELECT "first_name", "last_name", "age" FROM "Person"
    32→```
    33→
    34→### Selecting with Aliases
    35→
    36→Use aliases to rename columns in the result set:
    37→
    38→```cpp
    39→struct Result {
    40→    std::string name;
    41→    int person_age;
    42→};
    43→
    44→const auto query = select_from<Person>(
    45→    "first_name"_c | as<"name">,
    46→    "age"_c | as<"person_age">
    47→) | to<std::vector<Result>>;
    48→```
    49→
    50→This generates:
    51→```sql
    52→SELECT "first_name" AS "name", "age" AS "person_age" FROM "Person"
    53→```
    54→
    55→## Table Aliases
    56→
    57→### Aliased Tables
    58→
    59→When you need to reference the same table multiple times or want cleaner column references:
    60→
    61→```cpp
    62→const auto query = select_from<Person, "t1">(
    63→    "first_name"_t1,
    64→    "last_name"_t1,
    65→    "age"_t1
    66→) | where("age"_t1 > 18);
    67→```
    68→
    69→This generates:
    70→```sql
    71→SELECT t1."first_name", t1."last_name", t1."age" FROM "Person" t1 WHERE t1."age" > 18
    72→```
    73→
    74→## Selecting from Subqueries
    75→
    76→You can use the result of one query as the source for another query:
    77→
    78→```cpp
    79→// First, create a subquery
    80→const auto get_parents = select_from<Person, "t1">(
    81→    "child_id"_t2 | as<"id">,
    82→    "first_name"_t1 | as<"first_name">,
    83→    "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
    84→    "age"_t1 | as<"age">
    85→) | inner_join<Relationship, "t2">("id"_t1 == "parent_id"_t2);
    86→
    87→// Then use it as a source for another query
    88→const auto get_people = select_from<"t1">(
    89→    get_parents,  // Use the subquery as the source
    90→    "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
    91→    "first_name"_t1 | as<"first_name_parent">,
    92→    "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name_child">,
    93→    ("age"_t1 - "age"_t2) | as<"parent_age_at_birth">
    94→) | inner_join<Person, "t2">("id"_t1 == "id"_t2);
    95→```
    96→
    97→This generates:
    98→```sql
    99→SELECT t1."last_name" AS "last_name", t1."first_name" AS "first_name_parent", t2."first_name" AS "first_name_child", (t1."age") - (t2."age") AS "parent_age_at_birth" 
   100→FROM (
   101→    SELECT t2."child_id" AS "id", t1."first_name" AS "first_name", t1."last_name" AS "last_name", t1."age" AS "age" 
   102→    FROM "Person" t1 
   103→    INNER JOIN "Relationship" t2 ON t1."id" = t2."parent_id"
   104→) t1 
   105→INNER JOIN "Person" t2 ON t1."id" = t2."id"
   106→```
   107→
   108→## Expressions and Calculations
   109→
   110→You can select calculated expressions and literal values:
   111→
   112→```cpp
   113→struct Result {
   114→    std::string field;
   115→    double avg_field2;
   116→    std::optional<std::string> nullable_field;
   117→    int one;
   118→    std::string hello;
   119→};
   120→
   121→const auto query = select_from<TestTable>(
   122→    "field1"_c.as<"field">(),
   123→    avg("field2"_c).as<"avg_field2">(),
   124→    "nullable"_c | as<"nullable_field">,
   125→    as<"one">(1),                    // Literal value
   126→    "hello" | as<"hello">            // String literal
   127→) | to<Result>;
   128→```
   129→
   130→## Query Composition
   131→
   132→`select_from` can be combined with various query operations:
   133→
   134→```cpp
   135→const auto query = select_from<Person>(
   136→    "first_name"_c,
   137→    "last_name"_c,
   138→    "age"_c
   139→) 
   140→| where("age"_c >= 18)              // Filter results
   141→| order_by("last_name"_c, "first_name"_c)  // Order results
   142→| limit(10)                         // Limit number of results
   143→| to<std::vector<Person>>;          // Convert to container
   144→```
   145→
   146→### With Joins
   147→
   148→```cpp
   149→const auto query = select_from<Person, "t1">(
   150→    "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
   151→    "first_name"_t3 | as<"first_name_child">,
   152→    avg("age"_t1 - "age"_t3) | as<"avg_parent_age_at_birth">
   153→)
   154→| inner_join<Relationship, "t2">("id"_t1 == "parent_id"_t2)
   155→| inner_join<Person, "t3">("id"_t3 == "child_id"_t2)
   156→| group_by("last_name"_t1, "first_name"_t3)
   157→| order_by("last_name"_t1, "first_name"_t3)
   158→| to<std::vector<ParentAndChild>>;
   159→```
   160→
   161→## Result Type Conversion
   162→
   163→### Using `to<Container>`
   164→
   165→Convert query results to specific container types:
   166→
   167→```cpp
   168→// Convert to vector
   169→const auto people_vec = query | to<std::vector<Person>>;
   170→
   171→// Convert to single result (query must return exactly one row)
   172→const auto person = query | to<Person>;
   173→
   174→// Return as Range (lazy evaluation)
   175→const auto people_range = query;  // Returns Range<...> by default
   176→```
   177→
   178→### Automatic Type Deduction
   179→
   180→If you don't specify `to<...>`, `select_from` returns a `Range` type that can be iterated:
   181→
   182→```cpp
   183→const auto query = select_from<Person>("first_name"_c, "age"_c);
   184→
   185→// Execute and iterate
   186→for (const auto& result : sqlite::connect().and_then(query).value()) {
   187→    if (result) {
   188→        std::cout << result->first_name << ": " << result->age << std::endl;
   189→    }
   190→}
   191→```
   192→
   193→## Syntax Variations
   194→
   195→### Three Main Forms
   196→
   197→1. **Table without alias:**
   198→   ```cpp
   199→   select_from<TableType>(fields...)
   200→   ```
   201→
   202→2. **Table with alias:**
   203→   ```cpp
   204→   select_from<TableType, "t1">(fields...)
   205→   ```
   206→
   207→3. **Subquery with alias:**
   208→   ```cpp
   209→   select_from<"t1">(subquery, fields...)
   210→   ```
   211→
   212→## Column References
   213→
   214→Use the predefined column literals for clean syntax:
   215→
   216→```cpp
   217→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
   218→
   219→// Use _c for unaliased tables
   220→"column_name"_c
   221→
   222→// Use _t1, _t2, etc. for aliased tables/joins
   223→"column_name"_t1, "column_name"_t2
   224→
   225→// Or use explicit col syntax
   226→col<"column_name", "t1">
   227→```
   228→
   229→## Advanced Examples
   230→
   231→### Complex Nested Query
   232→
   233→```cpp
   234→struct ParentAndChild {
   235→    std::string last_name;
   236→    std::string first_name_parent;
   237→    std::string first_name_child;
   238→    double parent_age_at_birth;
   239→};
   240→
   241→// Step 1: Create a subquery to get parent-child relationships
   242→const auto get_children = select_from<Relationship, "t1">(
   243→    "parent_id"_t1 | as<"id">,
   244→    "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name">,
   245→    "age"_t2 | as<"age">
   246→) | inner_join<Person, "t2">("id"_t2 == "child_id"_t1);
   247→
   248→// Step 2: Use the subquery in a larger query
   249→const auto get_people = select_from<Person, "t1">(
   250→    "last_name"_t1 | as<"last_name">,
   251→    "first_name"_t1 | as<"first_name_parent">,
   252→    "first_name"_t2 | as<"first_name_child">,
   253→    ("age"_t1 - "age"_t2) | as<"parent_age_at_birth">
   254→) 
   255→| inner_join<"t2">(get_children, "id"_t1 == "id"_t2)
   256→| order_by("id"_t1, "id"_t2)
   257→| to<std::vector<ParentAndChild>>;
   258→```
   259→
   260→### Aggregation with Grouping
   261→

1→# `sqlgen::exec`
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen::exec` interface provides a way to execute raw SQL statements on a database connection. It's useful when you need to perform database operations that aren't covered by the type-safe interfaces, such as setting database-specific parameters or executing custom SQL statements.
     4→
     5→## Usage
     6→
     7→### Basic Execution
     8→
     9→Execute a raw SQL statement:
    10→
    11→```cpp
    12→const auto conn = sqlgen::postgres::connect(credentials);
    13→
    14→sqlgen::exec(conn, "SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';").value();
    15→```
    16→
    17→### Curried Execution
    18→
    19→You can also use a curried version of `exec` that takes the SQL statement first and returns a function that accepts the connection. This is useful for chaining operations:
    20→
    21→```cpp
    22→using namespace sqlgen;
    23→
    24→const auto query = exec("SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';");
    25→
    26→// Using with a connection reference
    27→const auto conn = postgres::connect(credentials);
    28→query(conn).value();
    29→
    30→// Or in a chain with other operations
    31→postgres::connect(credentials)
    32→    .and_then(exec("SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';"))
    33→    .value();
    34→```
    35→
    36→## Example: Full Query Composition
    37→
    38→Here's a complete example showing how to use `exec` within a chain of operations:
    39→
    40→```cpp
    41→using namespace sqlgen;
    42→
    43→const auto result = postgres::connect(credentials)
    44→    .and_then(exec("SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';"))
    45→    .and_then(drop<Person> | if_exists)
    46→    .and_then(write(people))
    47→    .and_then(read<std::vector<Person>>)
    48→    .value();
    49→```
    50→
    51→This executes the following SQL statements in sequence:
    52→
    53→```sql
    54→SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';
    55→DROP TABLE IF EXISTS "Person";
    56→-- Table creation and data insertion via write
    57→-- Data retrieval via read
    58→```
    59→
    60→## Notes
    61→
    62→- The `Result<Ref<Connection>>` type provides error handling; use `.value()` to extract the result (will throw an exception if there's an error) or handle errors as needed
    63→- The function has two overloads:
    64→  1. Takes a connection reference and SQL string
    65→  2. Takes a `Result<Ref<Connection>>` and SQL string
    66→- The curried version is particularly useful when you want to:
    67→  - Chain multiple database operations together
    68→  - Pass the execution operation as a function to other operations
    69→- Use `exec` when you need to:
    70→  - Execute database-specific commands
    71→  - Set database parameters
    72→  - Run custom SQL statements not covered by type-safe interfaces
    73→  - Perform administrative tasks
    74→- Exercise caution when using `exec` with user-provided input to prevent SQL injection attacks

1→# `sqlgen::exec`
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen::exec` interface provides a way to execute raw SQL statements on a database connection. It's useful when you need to perform database operations that aren't covered by the type-safe interfaces, such as setting database-specific parameters or executing custom SQL statements.
     4→
     5→## Usage
     6→
     7→### Basic Execution
     8→
     9→Execute a raw SQL statement:
    10→
    11→```cpp
    12→const auto conn = sqlgen::postgres::connect(credentials);
    13→
    14→sqlgen::exec(conn, "SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';").value();
    15→```
    16→
    17→### Curried Execution
    18→
    19→You can also use a curried version of `exec` that takes the SQL statement first and returns a function that accepts the connection. This is useful for chaining operations:
    20→
    21→```cpp
    22→using namespace sqlgen;
    23→
    24→const auto query = exec("SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';");
    25→
    26→// Using with a connection reference
    27→const auto conn = postgres::connect(credentials);
    28→query(conn).value();
    29→
    30→// Or in a chain with other operations
    31→postgres::connect(credentials)
    32→    .and_then(exec("SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';"))
    33→    .value();

     3→The `sqlgen::Result` type provides a way to handle errors without exceptions in sqlgen. It is an alias for `rfl::Result` and is used throughout sqlgen's API to handle potential failures in database operations.
     4→

     6→to resemble C++ 23's [std::expected](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/utility/expected).
     7→

    10→### Basic Usage
    11→
    12→Handle database operations that might fail:
    13→
    14→```cpp

    16→const auto people = sqlgen::read<std::vector<Person>>(conn);
    17→
    18→if (people) {
    19→    // Success case - use the value

    21→} else {
    22→    // Error case - handle the error
    23→    const auto& error = people.error();
    24→}
    25→
    26→// Writing to database
    27→const auto write_result = sqlgen::write(conn, data);
    28→
    29→if (!write_result) {
    30→    // Handle write error
    31→    const auto& error = write_result.error();
    32→}
    33→```
    34→
    35→### Monadic Operations
    36→
    37→The `Result` type supports several monadic operations for chaining operations:
    38→
    39→```cpp
    40→// Transform values (T -> U)
    41→const auto count = result.transform([](const auto& people) {
    42→    return people.size();
    43→});
    44→
    45→// Chain operations that might fail (T -> Result<U>)
    46→const auto processed = result.and_then([](const auto& people) {

    48→});
    49→

1→# `sqlgen::exec`
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen::exec` interface provides a way to execute raw SQL statements on a database connection. It's useful when you need to perform database operations that aren't covered by the type-safe interfaces, such as setting database-specific parameters or executing custom SQL statements.
     4→
     5→## Usage
     6→
     7→### Basic Execution
     8→
     9→Execute a raw SQL statement:
    10→
    11→```cpp
    12→const auto conn = sqlgen::postgres::connect(credentials);
    13→
    14→sqlgen::exec(conn, "SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';").value();
    15→```
    16→
    17→### Curried Execution
    18→
    19→You can also use a curried version of `exec` that takes the SQL statement first and returns a function that accepts the connection. This is useful for chaining operations:
    20→
    21→```cpp
    22→using namespace sqlgen;
    23→
    24→const auto query = exec("SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';");
    25→
    26→// Using with a connection reference
    27→const auto conn = postgres::connect(credentials);
    28→query(conn).value();
    29→
    30→// Or in a chain with other operations
    31→postgres::connect(credentials)
    32→    .and_then(exec("SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';"))
    33→    .value();
    34→```
    35→
    36→## Example: Full Query Composition
    37→
    38→Here's a complete example showing how to use `exec` within a chain of operations:
    39→
    40→```cpp
    41→using namespace sqlgen;
    42→
    43→const auto result = postgres::connect(credentials)
    44→    .and_then(exec("SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';"))
    45→    .and_then(drop<Person> | if_exists)
    46→    .and_then(write(people))
    47→    .and_then(read<std::vector<Person>>)
    48→    .value();
    49→```
    50→
    51→This executes the following SQL statements in sequence:
    52→
    53→```sql
    54→SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';
    55→DROP TABLE IF EXISTS "Person";
    56→-- Table creation and data insertion via write
    57→-- Data retrieval via read
    58→```
    59→
    60→## Notes
    61→
    62→- The `Result<Ref<Connection>>` type provides error handling; use `.value()` to extract the result (will throw an exception if there's an error) or handle errors as needed
    63→- The function has two overloads:
    64→  1. Takes a connection reference and SQL string
    65→  2. Takes a `Result<Ref<Connection>>` and SQL string
    66→- The curried version is particularly useful when you want to:
    67→  - Chain multiple database operations together
    68→  - Pass the execution operation as a function to other operations
    69→- Use `exec` when you need to:
    70→  - Execute database-specific commands
    71→  - Set database parameters
    72→  - Run custom SQL statements not covered by type-safe interfaces
    73→  - Perform administrative tasks
    74→- Exercise caution when using `exec` with user-provided input to prevent SQL injection attacks
    75→- The SQL statement is executed as-is, so ensure it's compatible with your database dialect
    76→

1→# `sqlgen::Timestamp`
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen::Timestamp` class provides a type-safe way to handle SQL timestamp fields in C++. It supports both regular timestamps and timestamps with time zones, with format validation at runtime. The class is essentially a wrapper around `std::tm` that adds format validation and SQL integration.
     4→
     5→## Usage
     6→
     7→### Basic Definition
     8→
     9→Define a timestamp field in your struct with a specific format:
    10→
    11→```cpp
    12→struct Person {
    13→    sqlgen::PrimaryKey<uint32_t> id;
    14→    std::string first_name;
    15→    std::string last_name;
    16→    sqlgen::Timestamp<"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"> birthdate;  // Regular timestamp
    17→    sqlgen::Timestamp<"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S%z"> created_at;  // Timestamp with timezone
    18→};
    19→```
    20→
    21→This generates the following SQL schema:
    22→
    23→```sql
    24→CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "Person"(
    25→    "id" INTEGER NOT NULL,
    26→    "first_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
    27→    "last_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
    28→    "birthdate" TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    29→    "created_at" TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE NOT NULL,
    30→    PRIMARY KEY ("id")
    31→);
    32→```
    33→
    34→### Construction and Assignment
    35→
    36→Create and assign timestamp values:
    37→
    38→```cpp
    39→// Direct string assignment
    40→Person person{
    41→    .id = 1,
    42→    .first_name = "Homer",
    43→    .last_name = "Simpson",
    44→    .birthdate = "1989-12-17 12:00:00",
    45→    .created_at = "2024-03-20 15:30:00+0000"
    46→};
    47→
    48→// Create from std::tm
    49→std::tm birth_tm = std::tm{};
    50→birth_tm.tm_year = 89;  // Years since 1900
    51→birth_tm.tm_mon = 11;   // 0-11 for months
    52→birth_tm.tm_mday = 17;  // Day of month
    53→birth_tm.tm_hour = 12;
    54→birth_tm.tm_min = 0;
    55→birth_tm.tm_sec = 0;
    56→sqlgen::Timestamp<"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"> birthdate(birth_tm);
    57→
    58→// Safe construction with error handling
    59→auto result = sqlgen::Timestamp<"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S">::from_string("1989-12-17 12:00:00");
    60→if (result) {
    61→    auto birthdate = result.value();
    62→    // Use birthdate...
    63→} else {
    64→    // Handle error...
    65→}
    66→```
    67→
    68→### Accessing Values
    69→
    70→Access the timestamp value in different formats:
    71→
    72→```cpp
    73→const auto person = Person{
    74→    .birthdate = "1989-12-17 12:00:00"
    75→};
    76→
    77→// Get as formatted string
    78→const std::string& str_value2 = person.birthdate.str(); // Returns "1989-12-17 12:00:00"
    79→
    80→// Get as std::tm for time operations
    81→const std::tm& tm_value = person.birthdate.tm();  // Direct access to underlying std::tm
    82→```
    83→
    84→### Time Zone Support
    85→
    86→The class supports both regular timestamps and timestamps with time zones:
    87→
    88→```cpp
    89→// Regular timestamp (without timezone)
    90→sqlgen::Timestamp<"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"> local_time;
    91→
    92→// Timestamp with timezone
    93→sqlgen::Timestamp<"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S%z"> utc_time;
    94→
    95→// Examples
    96→local_time = "2024-03-20 15:30:00";  // Local time
    97→utc_time = "2024-03-20 15:30:00+0000";  // UTC time with offset
    98→```
    99→
   100→## Format Specification
   101→
   102→The timestamp format is specified using a template parameter that follows the strftime format specifiers. This format is significant because:
   103→
   104→1. It defines the expected string format when reading timestamps from the database
   105→2. It determines how timestamps are formatted when writing to the database
   106→3. It enforces consistency between your C++ code and database storage
   107→
   108→For example, with this definition:
   109→```cpp
   110→struct Person {
   111→    sqlgen::Timestamp<"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"> birthdate;
   112→};
   113→```
   114→
   115→- When reading from the database, the timestamp must be in the format "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS"
   116→- When writing to the database, the timestamp will be formatted as "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS"
   117→- Any attempt to assign a string in a different format will throw a runtime error
   118→
   119→The most importand supported format specifiers are:
   120→
   121→- `%Y`: Year with century (e.g., 2024)
   122→- `%m`: Month (01-12)
   123→- `%d`: Day of month (01-31)
   124→- `%H`: Hour in 24h format (00-23)
   125→- `%M`: Minute (00-59)
   126→- `%S`: Second (00-59)
   127→- `%z`: Timezone offset (e.g., +0000, -0500)
   128→
   129→Please refer to https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/chrono/c/strftime for a comprehensive list of supported format specifiers.
   130→
   131→Common format patterns:
   132→- `"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"` for regular timestamps
   133→- `"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S%z"` for timestamps with timezone
   134→
   135→### Database Integration
   136→
   137→The format parameter ensures type safety and consistency in database operations:
   138→
   139→```cpp
   140→// Reading from database
   141→const auto people = sqlgen::read<std::vector<Person>>(conn).value();
   142→// All timestamps in 'people' will be in the format "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"
   143→
   144→// Writing to database
   145→const auto person = Person{
   146→    .birthdate = "1989-12-17 12:00:00"  // Must match the format
   147→};
   148→sqlgen::write(conn, person);  // Will be stored in the database in this format
   149→
   150→// Querying with timestamps
   151→const auto query = sqlgen::read<std::vector<Person>> | 
   152→                  where("birthdate"_c == "1989-12-17 12:00:00");  // Must match the format
   153→```
   154→
   155→This format validation helps prevent:
   156→- Data corruption from inconsistent timestamp formats
   157→- SQL injection by validating the format before database operations
   158→- Runtime errors from malformed timestamp strings
   159→
   160→## Notes
   161→
   162→- The template parameter `_format` specifies the expected timestamp format
   163→- Format validation occurs at runtime when values are assigned
   164→- The class is a wrapper around `std::tm` that adds:
   165→  - Format validation
   166→  - String conversion
   167→  - SQL integration
   168→  - Type safety
   169→- The class supports:
   170→  - Direct string assignment with format validation
   171→  - Construction from `std::tm`
   172→  - Safe construction with error handling via `from_string`
   173→  - Multiple access methods for the underlying value
   174→  - Direct access to the underlying `std::tm` via `tm()`
   175→  - Reflection for SQL operations
   176→  - Move and copy semantics
   177→- Timezone support varies by database:
   178→  - PostgreSQL supports both regular timestamps and timestamps with timezone
   179→  - SQLite treats all timestamps as UTC
   180→- The class uses the underlying `rfl::Timestamp` implementation for core functionality
   181→- All string operations are validated against the specified format
   182→- Invalid format strings will throw a runtime error
   183→- The class provides both compile-time and runtime safety

1→# `sqlgen::update` 
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen::update` interface provides a type-safe way to update records in a SQL database. It supports composable query building with `where` clauses to specify which records should be updated, and allows setting multiple columns to either literal values or other column values.
     4→
     5→## Usage
     6→
     7→### Basic Update
     8→
     9→Update specific columns in a table:
    10→
    11→```cpp
    12→const auto conn = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("database.db");
    13→
    14→using namespace sqlgen;
    15→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    16→
    17→const auto query = update<Person>("age"_c.set(100), "first_name"_c.set("New Name"));
    18→
    19→query(conn).value();
    20→```
    21→
    22→This generates the following SQL:
    23→
    24→```sql
    25→UPDATE "Person" 
    26→SET "age" = 100, "first_name" = 'New Name';
    27→```
    28→
    29→Note that `conn` is actually a connection wrapped into an `sqlgen::Result<...>`.
    30→This means you can use monadic error handling and fit this into a single line:
    31→
    32→```cpp
    33→// sqlgen::Result<Ref<Connection>>
    34→const auto result = sqlgen::sqlite::connect("database.db").and_then(
    35→                        update<Person>("age"_c.set(100), "first_name"_c.set("New Name")));
    36→```
    37→
    38→Please refer to the documentation on `sqlgen::Result<...>` for more information on error handling.
    39→
    40→### With `where` clause
    41→
    42→Update specific records using a `where` clause:
    43→
    44→```cpp
    45→using namespace sqlgen;
    46→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    47→
    48→const auto query = update<Person>("age"_c.set(100)) |
    49→                   where("first_name"_c == "Hugo");
    50→
    51→query(conn).value();
    52→```
    53→
    54→This generates the following SQL:
    55→
    56→```sql
    57→UPDATE "Person"
    58→SET "age" = 100
    59→WHERE "first_name" = 'Hugo';
    60→```
    61→
    62→Note that `"..."_c` refers to the name of the column. If such a field does not
    63→exist on the struct `Person`, the code will fail to compile. It is defined 
    64→in the namespace `sqlgen::literals`.
    65→
    66→You can also use monadic error handling here:
    67→
    68→```cpp
    69→using namespace sqlgen;
    70→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    71→
    72→const auto query = update<Person>("age"_c.set(100)) |
    73→                   where("first_name"_c == "Hugo");
    74→
    75→// sqlgen::Result<Ref<Connection>>
    76→const auto result = sqlite::connect("database.db").and_then(query);
    77→```
    78→
    79→### Setting Columns to Other Column Values
    80→
    81→You can set a column's value to another column's value:
    82→
    83→```cpp
    84→using namespace sqlgen;
    85→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
    86→
    87→const auto query = update<Person>("first_name"_c.set("last_name"_c)) |
    88→                   where("age"_c > 18);
    89→
    90→query(conn).value();
    91→```
    92→
    93→This generates the following SQL:
    94→
    95→```sql
    96→UPDATE "Person"
    97→SET "first_name" = "last_name"
    98→WHERE "age" > 18;
    99→```
   100→
   101→## Example: Full Query Composition
   102→
   103→```cpp
   104→using namespace sqlgen;
   105→using namespace sqlgen::literals;
   106→
   107→const auto query = update<Person>(
   108→                    "first_name"_c.set("last_name"_c),
   109→                    "age"_c.set(100)) |
   110→                   where("age"_c > 0);
   111→
   112→const auto result = query(conn);
   113→
   114→if (!result) {
   115→    // Error handling
   116→}
   117→```
   118→
   119→This generates the following SQL:
   120→
   121→```sql
   122→UPDATE "Person"
   123→SET 
   124→    "first_name" = "last_name",
   125→    "age" = 100
   126→WHERE "age" > 0;
   127→```
   128→
   129→It is strongly recommended that you use `using namespace sqlgen`
   130→and `using namespace sqlgen::literals`. However,
   131→if you do not want to do that, you can rewrite the example above as follows:
   132→
   133→```cpp
   134→const auto query = sqlgen::update<Person>(
   135→                    sqlgen::col<"first_name">.set(sqlgen::col<"last_name">),
   136→                    sqlgen::col<"age">.set(100)) |
   137→                   sqlgen::where(sqlgen::col<"age"> > 0);
   138→
   139→const auto result = query(conn);
   140→```
   141→
   142→## Notes
   143→
   144→- You must specify at least one column to update
   145→- The `where` clause is optional - if omitted, all records will be updated
   146→- The `Result<Ref<Connection>>` type provides error handling; use `.value()` to extract the result (will throw an exception if there's an error) or handle errors as needed or refer to the documentation on `sqlgen::Result<...>` for other forms of error handling
   147→- `"..."_c` refers to the name of the column. It is defined in the namespace `sqlgen::literals`.
   148→- You can set columns to either literal values or other column values
   149→- The update operation is atomic - either all specified columns are updated or none are

1→# `sqlgen::exec`
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen::exec` interface provides a way to execute raw SQL statements on a database connection. It's useful when you need to perform database operations that aren't covered by the type-safe interfaces, such as setting database-specific parameters or executing custom SQL statements.
     4→
     5→## Usage
     6→
     7→### Basic Execution
     8→
     9→Execute a raw SQL statement:
    10→
    11→```cpp
    12→const auto conn = sqlgen::postgres::connect(credentials);
    13→
    14→sqlgen::exec(conn, "SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';").value();
    15→```
    16→
    17→### Curried Execution
    18→
    19→You can also use a curried version of `exec` that takes the SQL statement first and returns a function that accepts the connection. This is useful for chaining operations:
    20→
    21→```cpp
    22→using namespace sqlgen;
    23→
    24→const auto query = exec("SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';");
    25→
    26→// Using with a connection reference
    27→const auto conn = postgres::connect(credentials);
    28→query(conn).value();
    29→
    30→// Or in a chain with other operations
    31→postgres::connect(credentials)
    32→    .and_then(exec("SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';"))
    33→    .value();
    34→```
    35→
    36→## Example: Full Query Composition
    37→
    38→Here's a complete example showing how to use `exec` within a chain of operations:
    39→
    40→```cpp
    41→using namespace sqlgen;
    42→
    43→const auto result = postgres::connect(credentials)
    44→    .and_then(exec("SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';"))
    45→    .and_then(drop<Person> | if_exists)
    46→    .and_then(write(people))
    47→    .and_then(read<std::vector<Person>>)
    48→    .value();
    49→```
    50→
    51→This executes the following SQL statements in sequence:
    52→
    53→```sql
    54→SET TIME ZONE 'UTC';
    55→DROP TABLE IF EXISTS "Person";
    56→-- Table creation and data insertion via write
    57→-- Data retrieval via read
    58→```
    59→
    60→## Notes
    61→
    62→- The `Result<Ref<Connection>>` type provides error handling; use `.value()` to extract the result (will throw an exception if there's an error) or handle errors as needed
    63→- The function has two overloads:
    64→  1. Takes a connection reference and SQL string
    65→  2. Takes a `Result<Ref<Connection>>` and SQL string
    66→- The curried version is particularly useful when you want to:
    67→  - Chain multiple database operations together
    68→  - Pass the execution operation as a function to other operations
    69→- Use `exec` when you need to:
    70→  - Execute database-specific commands
    71→  - Set database parameters
    72→  - Run custom SQL statements not covered by type-safe interfaces
    73→  - Perform administrative tasks
    74→- Exercise caution when using `exec` with user-provided input to prevent SQL injection attacks
    75→- The SQL statement is executed as-is, so ensure it's compatible with your database dialect
    76→

1→# Timestamp and Date/Time Functions
     2→
     3→The `sqlgen` library provides a comprehensive set of operations for working with timestamps, dates, and times. These functions allow you to extract date/time parts, perform arithmetic, and convert between types in a type-safe and composable way. All timestamp operations work with the `sqlgen::Timestamp<...>` type (including the provided aliases `Date` and `DateTime`).
     4→
     5→### Timestamp Types
     6→
     7→- `Timestamp<format>`: Represents a timestamp with a custom format (see `sqlgen::Timestamp`).
     8→- `Date`: Alias for `Timestamp<"%Y-%m-%d">` (date only).
     9→- `DateTime`: Alias for `Timestamp<"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S">` (date and time).
    10→
    11→---
    12→
    13→### Date/Time Extraction Functions
    14→
    15→These functions extract parts of a timestamp or date:
    16→
    17→- `year(ts)`: Extracts the year as an integer.
    18→- `month(ts)`: Extracts the month (1-12).
    19→- `day(ts)`: Extracts the day of the month (1-31).
    20→- `hour(ts)`: Extracts the hour (0-23).
    21→- `minute(ts)`: Extracts the minute (0-59).
    22→- `second(ts)`: Extracts the second (0-59).
    23→- `weekday(ts)`: Extracts the day of the week (0 = Sunday for SQLite, 0 = Monday for Postgres).
    24→
    25→```cpp
    26→year("birthday"_c) | as<"year">
    27→month("birthday"_c) | as<"month">
    28→day("birthday"_c) | as<"day">
    29→hour("birthday"_c) | as<"hour">
    30→minute("birthday"_c) | as<"minute">
    31→second("birthday"_c) | as<"second">
    32→weekday("birthday"_c) | as<"weekday">
    33→```
    34→
    35→---
    36→
    37→### Timestamp Arithmetic
    38→
    39→You can add or subtract durations (e.g., days, years, weeks, milliseconds) to/from timestamp columns using standard C++ chrono types:
    40→
    41→```cpp
    42→("birthday"_c + std::chrono::days(10)) | as<"birthday_plus_10">
    43→("birthday"_c + std::chrono::years(1) - std::chrono::weeks(2)) | as<"birthday_shifted">
    44→```

    50→### Days Between
    51→
    52→Calculates the number of days between two timestamps or dates:

    61→
    62→Converts a timestamp to the number of seconds since the Unix epoch:

    67→```
    68→

    70→
    71→### Timestamp Construction and Conversion
    72→
    73→You can construct or cast timestamps from strings or from extracted parts:
    74→
    75→```cpp
    76→cast<Date>(concat(cast<std::string>(year("birthday"_c)), "-", cast<std::string>(month("birthday"_c)), "-", cast<std::string>(day("birthday"_c)))) | as<"birthday_recreated">
    77→```

    79→---
    80→

    82→

    86→    Date birthday_recreated;
    87→    time_t birthday_unixepoch;
    88→    double age_in_days;
    89→    int hour;
    90→    int minute;
    91→    int second;
    92→    int weekday;
    93→};

    96→    ("birthday"_c + std::chrono::days(10)) | as<"birthday">,
    97→    (cast<Date>(concat(cast<std::string>(year("birthday"_c)), "-",
    98→                        cast<std::string>(month("birthday"_c)), "-",
    99→                        cast<std::string>(day("birthday"_c))))) | as<"birthday_recreated">,
   100→    days_between("birthday"_c, Date("2011-01-01")) | as<"age_in_days">,
   101→    unixepoch("birthday"_c + std::chrono::days(10)) | as<"birthday_unixepoch">,
   102→    hour("birthday"_c) | as<"hour">,
   103→    minute("birthday"_c) | as<"minute">,
   104→    second("birthday"_c) | as<"second">,

   113→SELECT datetime("birthday", '+10 days') AS "birthday", ...

   118→```

   122→### Notes
   123→
